item.title: Why Groundcover’s CEO says agents are the power users of observability
item.dc:creator: Chris J. Preimesberger
item.description:
An AI coding agent can write a patch in minutes. Ask it whether that patch slows down the API endpoint

The post Why Groundcover’s CEO says agents are the power users of observability appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
An AI coding agent can write a patch in minutes. Ask it whether that patch slows down the API endpoint your customers hit most, and suddenly it needs something that lives outside the repository. It needs to see how the software runs.

That’s the premise behind Groundcover, an observability platform that wants to put production telemetry in the hands of developers and their coding agents. Yes, you read that correctly.

In a conversation with The New Stack’s Frederic Lardinois at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon this month in Salt Lake City, Groundcover CEO and co-founder Shahar Azulay explained why he thinks the same data engineers use to troubleshoot an incident can help an agent write and test a better change in the first place.

Your new observability user is an agent

“Now agents are the power users of observability,” Azulay told TNS. 

Groundcover exposes telemetry through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), giving coding agents a way to query it while they work. An agent investigating a slow API, for example, could use traces to see which service accounts for most of the latency. A developer writing a test could use observed application behavior to pick a scenario customers actually encounter.

Groundcover uses that approach internally. Its coding agents pull context from the company’s own telemetry, and agents involved in code review can look at measurements from staging deployments. It’s a way to give a reviewer something concrete to check when a patch looks perfectly reasonable in a diff.

Agents also give engineers something new to monitor. Azulay contrasts a familiar application trace that follows a request across several microservices with an agent run that can span hours and thousands of tool calls. A trace that long can make a Kubernetes incident look like light reading. 

Developers may need to inspect prompts and tool calls or use evaluations to judge whether a run behaved as intended. A completed run tells you the agent stopped. The trace can help you figure out what it did along the way.

Less instrumentation work, more room for detail

Groundcover uses an eBPF sensor to collect application and infrastructure telemetry without requiring developers to add an SDK to every service. It also supports OpenTelemetry, so teams can keep sending the signals they already collect and add custom instrumentation where they need more detail. That gives developers a baseline for a new service and a way to get more specific when a particular path or business operation warrants it.

Where the data runs is part of the pitch. Groundcover’s bring-your-own-cloud model keeps telemetry and Groundcover’s agent operations in the customer’s cloud environment, Azulay said. Customers pay for the underlying infrastructure, and Groundcover manages the deployment. 

For teams weighing how much telemetry to retain, the model puts the infrastructure bill in their own account. It also matters when prompts or tool calls may contain sensitive customer data and teams want to keep that information under their control.

We also ask what happens when the platform starts acting on what it sees. Azulay points to Groundcover’s move into Kubernetes optimization, where the immediate work centers on cost and resilience. He sees a path from there to agents that can help address an incident on both sides of the deployment, proposing a code change and adjusting infrastructure configuration. The conversation also gets into the practical work of switching observability platforms, including what happens to the dashboards and monitors engineers have spent years building.

Watch the full KubeCon interview on The New Stack’s YouTube channel to hear how Groundcover uses its own telemetry in code reviews and why Azulay thinks the next generation of coding agents will be a regular part of the observability stack.

The post Why Groundcover’s CEO says agents are the power users of observability appeared first on The New Stack.

AI coding agents can write code, but can they tell how it performs? The New Stack interviewed Groundcover CEO Shahar Azulay about giving agents access to production telemetry to help them investigate problems, review patches and write better tests.

item.title: Google’s Gemini 4 Neon tripled its coding score without changing the model
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Google’s new Gemini 4 Neon resolved 12.8% of the SWE-sweep coding benchmark using the mini-SWE harness, but that score jumped

The post Google’s Gemini 4 Neon tripled its coding score without changing the model appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Google’s new Gemini 4 Neon resolved 12.8% of the SWE-sweep coding benchmark using the mini-SWE harness, but that score jumped to 39.0% when the same model ran inside Antigravity.

The more-than-threefold improvement raises questions about how much coding-agent performance comes from the underlying model and how much depends on the harness…

Both results were reported Wednesday as part of the Neon launch. The more-than-threefold improvement raises questions about how much coding-agent performance comes from the underlying model and how much depends on the harness managing its tools, context, and execution.

A day earlier, a FrontierHarness benchmark found that running the same open model could cost up to five times more depending on the harness

Same model, different scores

Google’s Gemini 4 Neon model card compares three frontier models on SWE-sweep using their respective provider harnesses and a shared mini-SWE baseline.

Neon and Opus performed substantially better with their providers’ harnesses, but Sol did not.

Claude Opus 5.5 climbed from 3.6% with mini-SWE to 10.1% with Claude Code, while GPT-6.2 Sol went the other way, falling from 11.6% with mini-SWE to 8.3% with Codex. Neon and Opus performed substantially better with their providers’ harnesses, but Sol did not.

Google tested each model in two harness configurations, though the comparison does not isolate which changes account for the differences or whether the results would hold up across other benchmarks and repositories.

The harness does the work

Antigravity’s harness was co-trained with Gemini, and Neon has been updated to make fewer unnecessary file reads and better manage context during long coding sessions. Antigravity can also run subagents in separate Git worktrees and verify their changes.

Google only tested Neon against mini-SWE, so there’s no data yet on how it performs with other harnesses.

It’s unclear which of those changes contributed most to the SWE-sweep improvement, since they weren’t tested separately. Google only tested Neon against mini-SWE, so there’s no data yet on how it performs with other harnesses.

Neon plans, Hydrogen builds

Neon is joining the model-switching system Google introduced with Gemini 4 Hydrogen. It handles planning and harder coding problems, leaving routine work to Hydrogen, and can run multiple Hydrogen subagents in parallel using the /swarm feature introduced with Carbon.

Google hasn’t said how much this setup affects Neon’s SWE-sweep results or what it means for the cost of completing a task.

Counting the cost per task

The company reports that Neon scored 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 and 46.2% on FrontierCode 2.0 at its default high reasoning setting. It also topped the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index with a score of 58.6.

At its default high thinking level, the model costs 32% less per task than Gemini 4 Carbon, according to Google’s comparison using the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. API pricing is $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, with cached input at $0.15 per million tokens and a 1 million-token context window.

Neon is available through the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, and Gemini for Business. Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers can also access it through Antigravity.

Gemini 4 Neon scored 12.8% on SWE-sweep alone but 39% inside Antigravity — a jump that shows how much a coding agent’s harness shapes its benchmark score.

item.title: Microsoft says Bing serves 1B people. Its next search engine isn’t for them.
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
Microsoft says its Bing search engine now has one billion monthly users. The company says those are humans — not

The post Microsoft says Bing serves 1B people. Its next search engine isn’t for them. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft says its Bing search engine now has one billion monthly users. The company says those are humans — not AI agents — looking up information on the web. What most people may not realize, though, is that Microsoft also uses the same Bing index to serve agents through Web IQ.

Web IQ is Microsoft’s agentic search service, competing with upstarts like Exa, Firecrawl, and Tavily. DeepSeek opened its own search API to developers in October.

At Microsoft’s Ignite conference this week in San Francisco, The New Stack sat down with Jordi Ribas, Microsoft’s president of Search & AI. Ribas joined the search team in 2008, back when Bing was still called Live Search. Today, his team runs both Bing and Web IQ, which Microsoft introduced at Build in June and opened broadly to Azure customers on Tuesday.

How agents search differently

“Bing is a search engine for humans,” Ribas says. “This is really [a] search engine where the queries come from the AI, and so you do need to design it differently because agents search differently.”

“Bing is a search engine for humans.”

It’s not just that human and agent search queries look different (and Ribas noted that agent searches often look a bit “robotic”), but that they also have different expectations for the results.

On Bing, Ribas says, the order of the results matters because people have to decide which link to click. “An agent doesn’t really need that,” he says, “because an agent will read everything.”

At their core, Bing and Web IQ share the part of the search engine that finds the relevant documents, Ribas says. For agents, Web IQ picks out the passages it deems most relevant and sends them back.

For example, an agent comparing corporate earnings results might need only one row in a table on page 12. Sending the whole report would give the agent more context than it needs, and because the model would have to wade through far more text, the search would become far more expensive.

As Ribas puts it, “the agent will spend money basically by reading all the documents.” “So it’s very important that you extract exactly what you need, and no more.”

Microsoft builds that shared index, always follows the instructions in a site’s robots.txt file, and identifies itself as a crawler, Ribas stressed multiple times. “Not everybody does that in the space.”

How much of the search should the agent do?

Typically, the agent’s orchestrator decides when to call Web IQ as a tool and what queries to send, Ribas notes. “Sometimes the orchestrator is not that smart about knowing what queries to do,” he says, “and it may do multiple iterations.”

At Ignite, Microsoft is addressing this by making Auto the default search mode in Web IQ, which Ribas describes as “kind of like a mini orchestrator that happens within Web IQ.”

With this change, an agent sends Web IQ only one question. Microsoft then tries a few variations of the query in parallel and sends back passages with citations.

Auto Advanced takes this a step further and checks whether the first round turned up enough information. If it finds a gap, it revises the query and searches again. “And we do have a model that says, ‘OK, is that evidence enough to provide a good chat response?'” Ribas says. “And if it’s yes, great, we’re done.”

Unlike some Web IQ competitors that try to create full answers and research reports themselves, Microsoft leaves the agents and models that power them to create the actual answers.

“You can use pretty much any model on top of it,” Ribas says, though he adds that Microsoft is thinking about packaging Web IQ with a model at some point.

What Web IQ costs

On Web IQ, one thousand standard web searches cost $7, compared with $8 for Auto and $9 for Auto Advanced. (The $1 starting price Microsoft advertises is for Browse, where you already have the URL.) If you know exactly what you’re looking for, the standard search may be all you need. But if your agent routinely reads the results, rewrites the query and tries again, a single Auto call could cost less overall.

“If you want to be fast but you want higher quality, maybe Auto is the way to go.”

“If all you care is about being super fast, then you would just use maybe the primitives directly,” Ribas says, referring to the individual search APIs. “If you want to be fast but you want higher quality, maybe Auto is the way to go.”

A crowded agent search market

“People are predicting that in a couple of years there will be 1,000 times more queries done by agents than by humans,” Ribas says. “That’s why there are so many competitors in [the] space.”

Some of those competitors optimize for quality, Ribas says, but “bring a lot of tokens to come up with a comprehensive answer,” which drives up both cost and latency. Others, he says, are very fast, but the quality isn’t there.

“We are able to optimize across three dimensions: quality, latency, and token efficiency,” he says, “and that’s really hard to do.”

Genspark co-founder Ray Zhong says in Microsoft’s announcement that switching to Web IQ cut its voice assistant’s response time from six seconds to 0.6 seconds. “Six seconds in a voice turn is audible dead air.”

The post Microsoft says Bing serves 1B people. Its next search engine isn’t for them. appeared first on The New Stack.
Bing serves a billion humans. Microsoft’s Web IQ feeds agents from the same index, but trims results to the exact passages a model needs to read.

item.title: “The best escape room players that you’ve ever met”: What Red Hat’s AI architect really thinks about agents.
item.dc:creator: Steven J. Vaughan-Nichols
item.description:
Last week at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America, a major gathering of the open-source and cloud-native communities, many speakers —

The post “The best escape room players that you’ve ever met”: What Red Hat’s AI architect really thinks about agents. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Last week at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America, a major gathering of the open-source and cloud-native communities, many speakers — when they weren’t contemplating what the then-rapidly unfolding Nvidia fiasco would mean for them — worried about AI security. 

Hence, all the coverage of OpenShell and Agent Substrate. So it fit the mood when Jessica Forrester, Red Hat’s chief architect of AI Catalyst Engineering, opened her keynote at the Salt Palace Convention Center in Salt Lake City by calling AI agents “the best escape room players that you’ve ever met.”

She was talking about agents “that take feature requests all the way to code.”

“Give them a goal, and they will try every drawer, every picture frame, and every door until something works. It’s what makes them great at writing code,” Forrester explained.

She continued: “It’s also what keeps me up at night, because to a player like that, everything in the room looks like a part of the puzzle, and sometimes they’ll even decide the puzzle is something else entirely.”

“…to a player like that, everything in the room looks like a part of the puzzle, and sometimes they’ll even decide the puzzle is something else entirely.”

Forrester’s right. That is scary. 

It’s not a theoretical problem either. Just ask SaaStr founder Jason Lemkin, whose Replit agent deleted a live production database. He restored the database using Replit’s built-in rollback feature after the same agent assured him it couldn’t be done. Unless we take precautions, we’ll see this same scenario, and worse, play out again.

Forrester explained, using an escape room metaphor, that when you set an agent a task, it will try any and all means to accomplish it. In one run, she said, the agent “decided that it wanted to come up with a bunch of brand new ideas. It wasn’t attacked or compromised; it just drifted.”

“From the outside, a confused agent and a compromised agent look exactly the same.”

The result, she continued, was that “From the outside, a confused agent and a compromised agent look exactly the same. They’re both pulling on doors that you didn’t intend for them to, and behind one of them could be your production database. So we assume the agent is already compromised, and we build our platform up from there.”

That’s a good approach. Forrester also adds that relying on prompts alone to keep an agent in bounds isn’t enough.

“Prompts are like signs. Policies are like bolts, but don’t leave a screwdriver in the room because anything you do leave, the agent might use.”

“Some escape rooms will put signs in the room, like ‘Please don’t move the picture frames.’ This doesn’t work. Instead, they bolt them onto the wall.

“Prompts are like signs. Policies are like bolts, but don’t leave a screwdriver in the room because anything you do leave, the agent might use.”

So what does that mean in practice? In her demo, the agent’s network access was restricted to its model and GitHub. Forrester explained that “OpenShell is an open-source sandbox for AI agents. Its policies are the bolts.

“Aside from talking to its model, the agent can do one thing: read from GitHub. Its task is to go get a particular README for the escape room and follow its instructions, whatever it finds. Reading from GitHub was allowed, so this works.” 

But when the agent tries to reach a destination the policy doesn’t allow, OpenShell blocks it and logs the attempt. With its policy advisor enabled, the agent can propose a new network rule to request additional access. Those proposals require human approval by default; the agent can’t approve its own request.

In a theCUBE interview at the same event, Forrester added that “With OpenShell, your agent doesn’t ever get any real keys to anything. It gets masked on the way in and then swapped on the way out.” That means, “If something convinces it to give away its keys, it’s not actually giving any real keys away. That really helps you have a little bit more faith in what’s happening inside that agent box.” 

As Red Hat itself explained in its technical description of OpenShell, “OpenShell runs your agent inside a sandbox governed by a policy you write. The policy covers network egress, filesystem access, and process privileges. Anything it doesn’t explicitly allow is denied.” 

Still, as Forrester observed in her keynote, “our bolts can only hold if the wall itself holds.”  That matters if an external attacker or a rogue or misbehaving agent targets the environment OpenShell runs in.

To protect against that, Forrester’s team runs its agent sandboxes in Kata Containers. In Kata, container workloads run on lightweight VMs, which use hardware-backed isolation and their own Linux kernel. In short, containers work as usual, but they run within a VM security box. 

“Assume the agent is already compromised, and that it will try every door.”

“This way, our agents, all of our agents, get their own kernel,” Forrester explained. “Even then, we don’t actually give our agents real keys. They look real to them, but they open nothing, and they’re almost like a prop. OpenShell is swapping in the real key on the way out the door. This way, if someone convinces our agent to hand over its keys some other way, all it’s handing over is a prop.”

Are we right to be a little paranoid? Well, yes.

Forrester put it this way: “Assume the agent is already compromised, and that it will try every door.”

But given how much damage an agent can cause, most may agree that the more control we have over them, the better.

The post “The best escape room players that you’ve ever met”: What Red Hat’s AI architect really thinks about agents. appeared first on The New Stack.
Red Hat’s Jessica Forrester says AI agents act like escape room players. Her fix: assume they’re compromised and bolt them in with sandboxes and fake keys.

item.title: Qwen4-Max vs. Claude Opus 5.5: The cheaper model costs you somewhere else.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Wachtel
item.description:
Qwen4-Max, made available in preview to Token Plan subscribers on November 11 and generally released on November 16, is quite

The post Qwen4-Max vs. Claude Opus 5.5: The cheaper model costs you somewhere else. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Qwen4-Max, made available in preview to Token Plan subscribers on November 11 and generally released on November 16, is quite the talker.

When the independent testing firm Artificial Analysis ran its standard test suite on Alibaba’s new model, Qwen4-Max generated 127 million output tokens. That’s roughly twice the median for comparable models. Artificial Analysis reports 218 million output tokens for Claude Opus 5.5 at max effort with default fallback enabled. That is more than Qwen4-Max uses, but Opus’s default effort setting is medium.

Writing a lot of tokens doesn’t automatically mean a higher bill, especially with Qwen4-Max, because Alibaba charges very little for those tokens. Qwen4-Max costs $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens. Claude Opus 5.5 costs more, billing at $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens. Cached input has separate pricing: Qwen4-Max lists $0.075 per million cached input tokens, while Opus 5.5 cache reads cost $0.20 per million tokens. Cache writes also have separate rates.

Cheaper only wins if you don’t give up accuracy to get it.

Costs and tokens are only part of the picture, though. Cheaper only wins if you don’t give up accuracy to get it. Alibaba’s launch post calls Qwen4-Max “your new teammate,” which I take to mean it’s positioned as an everyday workhorse. Alibaba’s launch chart shows wins and losses against Opus on agent benchmarks, where a model works through a job step by step using tools. Its coding results are mixed too: Qwen4-Max trails Opus 48.5% to 59.6% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, but leads on DeepSWE v1.1. These published results use different benchmarks and evaluation setups; they are not a single controlled comparison.

I’ve seen fact and fiction in launch marketing materials (including benchmarks), so I wanted to get to the bottom of this. Is Qwen4-Max a better alternative to Opus 5.5 for some day-to-day work? I ran a few tests to answer that question for everyday users.

The tests

I ran each model once per test at default settings, with no turn cap. Opus 5.5 ran through Anthropic’s API, and Qwen4-Max ran through OpenRouter on Alibaba’s own servers. Opus’s dollar figures are estimates based on reported token usage and Anthropic’s list prices. Qwen4-Max’s are what OpenRouter billed. The aggregate token totals below don’t separate uncached input, cache writes, and cache reads, so they aren’t sufficient to independently reproduce the cost estimates. I wrote a script that graded each model’s answers against an answer key I built along with the tests.

I wanted to make sure the tests were hard for each model, so I used GPT-5 as a baseline and ran each test through it first. When GPT-5’s score was low enough to count as a failure, I considered the test “hard enough.”

Here are the three tests I used:

  • Multi-app workflow (76 points) – I set up a fake company with a ticket tracker, code repo, chat, and calendar, and each model worked across all four as an agent. It had to triage a customer bug, find the code change that caused it, assign the right owner, calculate deadlines, count tickets, and refuse two requests that company policy forbids.
  • Incident investigation (60 points) – The models had to dig through logs, metrics, and change history to explain three overlapping outages that happened at the same time. The data included decoy deploys, two servers with wrong clocks, and a misleading alert.
  • Agent bug fix (47 points) – Each model fixed an accounting library with 11 planted bugs. Six of those bugs don’t fail any test the model can see, so it had to find them by comparing the code with the documentation. Three of the library’s own tests are wrong, and the model should report them without editing them.

Multi-app workflow

Opus 5.5 scored all 76 points. Qwen4-Max scored 71.

All five of Qwen4-Max’s missed points came from the same mistake. Three questions asked which team owns a piece of code. The repo’s ownership file says that when several rules match, the last one in the file wins. Qwen4-Max picked the most specific rule each time. Everything else it did was correct, including the deadline math across time zones and both refusals.

…Qwen4-Max can handle a long, messy office job, but one misread rule followed it through the whole task.

That tells me Qwen4-Max can handle a long, messy office job, but one misread rule followed it through the whole task. In a real company, that mistake sends tickets to the wrong team, creating more confusion.

Qwen4-Max wrote almost twice as many output tokens as Opus but cost less than a third. It also took more than three times as long for a little more than half as many turns.

The numbers:

  • Opus 5.5: 44 turns, 2,451,342 in, 26,617 out, $2.13, 248 s.
  • Qwen4-Max: 25 turns, 1,746,170 in, 51,264 out (41,644 reasoning), $0.62, 791 s.

Incident investigation

Qwen4-Max narrowly pulled ahead on accuracy here. It scored 59 of 60, and Opus 5.5 scored 58.

Both models untangled the three outages, named the two-step cause of the main one, ruled out every decoy, and caught both bad clocks. Both also made the same kind of slip. They credited a customer-facing error code to the wrong service, Opus twice and Qwen4-Max once.

This was Qwen4-Max’s strongest result in my tests. On this investigation task, it scored one point higher than Opus for about 31% of the reported cost. One run does not establish a general advantage in agent work. Opus 5.5 pulled ahead on time, though. Qwen4-Max took about 9.5 minutes, and Opus took under 4.

The numbers:

  • Opus 5.5: 22 turns, 1,216,769 in, 23,642 out, $1.41, 221 s.
  • Qwen4-Max: 18 turns, 1,104,031 in, 33,036 out (23,153 reasoning), $0.44, 570 s.

Agent bug fix

Just like the last test, neither model scored perfectly on accuracy. Opus 5.5 scored 45 of 47, and Qwen4-Max scored 40. This was the coding test, and its result was consistent with Opus’s lead on Terminal-Bench 4.0, though Alibaba’s coding results were mixed.

Opus fixed all 11 bugs. Its only miss was the third wrong test, which it didn’t report, costing it two points. Qwen4-Max missed that same test and lost five more points. It fixed 10 of the 11 bugs and missed one where splitting a payment across invoices loses a cent. It also left a scratch file in the tests folder, which my rules count as changing the tests.

The tool logs show how differently they worked. Opus made its first fix on turn 4 and finished in 12 turns. Qwen4-Max read files for 15 turns before its first edit and took 30 turns in all. More reading didn’t translate to a better score in this case, though.

The cost gap was smallest on this test. Qwen4-Max used more than three times the input tokens, so its bill came to about two-thirds of Opus’s.

The numbers:

  • Opus 5.5: 12 turns, 228,824 in, 6,433 out, $0.38, 64 s.
  • Qwen4-Max: 30 turns, 827,545 in, 15,813 out (6,701 reasoning), $0.25, 310 s.

Results

The talker reputation checked out. Qwen4-Max generated 77% more output tokens than Opus across the three tests. Those totals include reasoning tokens, so they do not measure just the length of the visible answers; the models also use different tokenizers.

What Qwen4-Max really costs is time and accuracy.

Its prices are low enough that it didn’t matter, and the total bill still came to about a third of Opus’s. What Qwen4-Max really costs is time and accuracy. It took about 3.14 times as long in total and scored 170 of 183 points, nine fewer than Opus’s 179.

What do I think?

Each model ran once, so a gap of a point or two could shift on another run. I’d try Qwen4-Max on your own long-running agent jobs before trusting it with code. I recommend checking its answers against source material and verifying code with tests and human review; a second model’s agreement alone does not establish accuracy.

I’d keep Opus 5.5 for coding and for any job where a wrong answer could cause problems down the line. It was more accurate on two of the three tests, and it finished the three tasks in about a third of the total time.

Qwen4-Max earned a place, though. For investigation work, where the model digs through a lot of data and can wait a few extra minutes, it matched Opus for a fraction of the price. Qwen4-Max’s one-point lead on this investigation task is encouraging, but these single-run tests cannot validate Alibaba’s broader agent claims or establish a general coding ranking.

The post Qwen4-Max vs. Claude Opus 5.5: The cheaper model costs you somewhere else. appeared first on The New Stack.

Alibaba’s benchmark chart shows mixed results for Qwen4-Max against Claude Opus 5.5 on agent work. In hands-on tests, Qwen4-Max beat Opus 5.5 by one point on one agent test but lost the other two. Qwen4-Max cost about two-thirds less and took 214% longer to complete the tasks.

item.title: OpenAI spent $1.2 million finding nearly 1,000 Linux security flaws. Sam Altman says this is just the beginning.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
OpenAI spent approximately $1.2 million in API costs to generate working exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities. At The New

The post OpenAI spent $1.2 million finding nearly 1,000 Linux security flaws. Sam Altman says this is just the beginning. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI spent approximately $1.2 million in API costs to generate working exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities. At The New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday, CEO Sam Altman pointed to those results as an example of what developers could accomplish by spending substantially more on compute to solve difficult engineering problems.

“Apply that to optimizing your code, apply that to solving other hard problems. All that’s coming,” Altman says, appearing alongside OpenAI President Greg Brockman.

The Linux research is part of OpenAI’s broader investment in compute-intensive AI, which includes custom chips, infrastructure, and an agent platform that Altman wants developers to use. He believes the biggest constraint on what these systems can accomplish will be the compute available to run them.

Hunting kernel bugs at scale

In a November 4 technical report titled “A thousand fewer paths to root,” OpenAI says its automated pipeline reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, then generated working exploits for more than half of them.

The agents searched for vulnerabilities, but also, reproduced bugs, tested whether they could be exploited, and wrote patches. Human security researchers reviewed the findings before sending them to Linux kernel maintainers, though OpenAI’s reported numbers do not mean all 948 vulnerabilities have been independently verified or fixed.

The company says the roughly $1.2 million in API spending represents an upper bound because the team had not optimized its harness for cost efficiency.

The results demonstrate how much engineering work agents can perform when given substantial inference budgets. OpenAI is also developing long-running agents that can consume thousands of dollars in compute per day.

OpenAI wants to own the AI stack

“I think we are set up to be like vertically integrated, to deliver the best thing across all the ways people need to use it, and we’re thrilled for people to build very successful businesses on top of us,” Altman says.

OpenAI has spent months investing across custom silicon, computing infrastructure, frontier models, and an agent platform designed to serve consumers and enterprises. The company has also moved further down the stack with its own silicon.

“We are the only company that has the entire intelligence stack.”

Altman made a broader claim about OpenAI’s position in the industry. “We are the only company that has the entire intelligence stack,” he says.

A custom chip for inference

OpenAI’s custom Jalapeño inference chip is already in development, with early reported benchmarks showing gains in throughput per watt and token latency. At DealBook, Altman made an even bigger claim about its potential.

“We have our own chip coming, which is I think going to be the best inference chip in the industry.”

“We have our own chip coming, which is I think going to be the best inference chip in the industry,” Altman says.

The company also wants to bring more of its software offerings together.

“My focus and our focus on product’s been to have one agentic platform that you’re getting everyone to use,” Altman says.

Altman did not announce changes to OpenAI’s developer APIs or restrictions on third-party applications, and he offered few technical details about how the proposed platform would operate.

Compute is the real limiter

Altman believes AI models will become essential to running businesses, but how much companies can do with them will depend on the compute they can access. Recent coding-agent harness comparisons have shown how much execution costs can vary depending on the software surrounding a model.

“I think that the biggest limiter really just will be compute.”

“I think that the economy again is going to be massively accelerated through this technology,” he says. “I think that the biggest limiter really just will be compute.”

item.title: AI needs fresh data. Vector indexing is getting in the way
item.dc:creator: Meredith Shubel
item.description:
It’s not a revelation to say AI workflows are changing enterprise infrastructure. What gets less attention, though, is how they’re

The post AI needs fresh data. Vector indexing is getting in the way appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
It’s not a revelation to say AI workflows are changing enterprise infrastructure. What gets less attention, though, is how they’re also shifting the fundamentals of data processing and search.

The complication lies in the data. As organizations build generative AI (GenAI) applications, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems, and AI agents, they’re generating an unwieldy number of vectors from growing volumes of unstructured data. And with all that vectorized data comes a challenge: how to quickly find the right information to power AI applications and workflows. 

“After all, a model can only reason over the context you can find and feed it.”

Whether it’s a RAG system answering a question or an AI agent taking action, enterprise AI applications succeed on retrieval. After all, a model can only reason over the context you can find and feed it. If those systems rely on wrong or outdated information, even the best model can’t fix the underlying context problem. 

But finding the right context inside petabytes of enterprise data is a difficult search problem — one keyword search alone is no match. 

Search has moved beyond keywords

In recent years, search has come a long way from basic keyword-based matching. For one, user behavior has spearheaded a push from simple keyword entries to natural language queries. Agent workloads, meanwhile, which query 10 to 100 times more than humans, bring a new dimension to search — and traditional databases are not prepared to keep up.

While full-text search uses analyzers and relevance tuning to find exact words and phrases that match the index, semantic search goes beyond keywords to focus on meaning and intent, letting users search with everyday language or synonyms instead of exact index terms. Vector search, meanwhile, enables similarity search, using vector embeddings (i.e., numerical representations of data) stored in vector fields to find items that are semantically similar rather than exact matches. 

Hybrid search joins keyword and vector search, letting users combine exact keyword matches with meaning-based searches in a single result set. 

In the new phase of AI adoption, where applications increasingly rely on swathes of unstructured data to retrieve context, traditional keyword search is no longer enough to surface the right information on its own. As a result, organizations are increasingly turning to high-performance vector databases, semantic search, and hybrid search to support new AI workloads. 

Therein lies the next challenge: indexing all those vectors so they can be searched.

Why indexing is the new bottleneck

As organizations move from gigabyte-scale search to petabyte-scale AI workloads, the ability to quickly index vectors has become a major factor in determining whether AI applications have current information to work with. 

The problem is, indexing is often a slow, compute-intensive process, which means it can take days or even weeks for incoming vectors to become searchable. 

“For customers who want to search across petabytes of data, they may notice that it takes days to weeks to index.”

As Rachael Wade, global tech alliances manager at Elastic, tells The New Stack, “For customers who want to search across petabytes of data, they may notice that it takes days to weeks to index.” While a longer indexing timetable may work fine for smaller AI pilots, once it’s time to move those projects into production, indexing delays can significantly stall deployment timelines. 

A big part of the challenge lies in building the vector index, or HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) graph, a layered data structure that connects similar vectors to enable efficient search. During construction, vectors must be compared to determine how they should connect in the graph. Because this process can involve millions or even billions of vectors, building a vector index at enterprise scale is compute-intensive and requires a dizzying number of mathematical operations. 

What happens when enterprises don’t have the compute to keep up? Indexing is slow, so new information takes longer to become searchable, leaving RAG systems, queries, and agents potentially working on stale data. 

“…the new constraint is getting vectors indexed fast enough to keep that search current.”

One example Wade points out to The New Stack is a product catalog, where e-commerce companies rely on fresh data to keep production information up to date and searchable. Manas Singh, technical product manager for accelerated ML and vector search at Nvidia, agrees, adding that, for many companies, “the new constraint is getting vectors indexed fast enough to keep that search current.”

It’s time for GPU-accelerated indexing

While CPUs have been the default for building vector indexes, IT leaders are starting to realize that CPU-based indexing can struggle to meet the scale and data-freshness requirements of modern AI workloads. 

For one, indexing vectorized data at petabyte scale can be painstakingly slow, taking days or even weeks. It’s also costly; when you need to index hundreds of millions or billions of vectors, CPU hardware expenses can add up fast. 

But where CPU-based indexing can be slow and expensive at scale, GPUs are designed for this very kind of large-scale, high-intensity work. For AI workloads with large data volumes and high ingest rates, that makes accelerated computing GPUs built for massive parallelism and high-throughput math ideally positioned for the job. 

At least that’s the idea behind Elastic and Nvidia’s collaboration on GPU-accelerated vector indexing for Elasticsearch. 

The integration is powered by Nvidia cuVS, an open-source NVIDIA CUDA-XTM library for GPU-accelerated vector search and data clustering that enables faster index building and embedding retrieval for AI and recommendation workloads. Elasticsearch accesses cuVS through cuvs-java, another open-source library maintained by Nvidia.

Elastic, for its part, brings semantic and hybrid search to the table via its enterprise-focused vector database — one of the most widely used in the world that powers semantic search, AI assistants, and recommendations for both startups and enterprises. Developers can trial Elasticsearch for free.

By accelerating vector indexing, the Elastic and Nvidia collaboration aims to help enterprises index massive volumes of vectorized data faster so it becomes available sooner for semantic search and AI workloads, including GenAI and AI agents, at speed and scale. 

The payoff of faster indexing can be substantial. Per Elastic, moving indexing construction to GPU with Nvidia cuVS delivers nearly a 12x boost in indexing throughput and a 7x reduction in force-merge latency, i.e., the time it takes to consolidate small index segments.

To put the cost difference in perspective, Wade points to a cost-model example comparing a GPU-based setup with CPU infrastructure. As she tells The New Stack, one GPU, depending on the model, can index hundreds of millions of vectors within a roughly 10-minute SLA. Doing the same work with CPUs, she says, would take about 10 CPUs and require roughly two hours — amounting to what she says is a baseline total cost of ownership savings of 78%. 

The benefits of GPU acceleration become even more pronounced as vector dimensions increase. Because CPUs take significantly longer to process vectors at higher dimensions, GPU acceleration — whether that’s 5x, 6x, 7x, or even 12x — becomes more valuable at larger scales. 

Why faster indexing matters now

For on-premises deployments, Singh also highlights the indirect benefit of lower search latency. 

By shifting indexing work from CPUs to faster, more efficient GPUs, enterprises can free up CPUs for other work, thereby allowing the same on-premises hardware to dedicate more resources to search operations. As Singh puts it: “You free up the CPU resources for other things,” which he says can ultimately lead to lower search latency. 

Meanwhile, because GPU-accelerated vector indexing is available in self-managed Elasticsearch environments, including on-premises, developers can take advantage of faster indexing without having to move workloads off infrastructure they control. 

Altogether, for IT leaders evaluating hardware with an eye on maximizing ROI and maintaining data sovereignty, that means moving indexing from CPUs to GPUs is a triple win: It can complete more indexing work in less time with less infrastructure, while also meeting self-managed, on-premises deployment requirements and freeing up CPU capacity for search. 

In the bigger picture, the move toward GPU-accelerated indexing reflects how AI is changing data processing and search. For RAG systems, AI agents, and other retrieval-dependent applications, getting new data searchable quickly is critical to making those systems truly useful. And that starts with faster indexing.

As vector workloads grow, Elastic and Nvidia are shifting index construction to accelerate AI, boost throughput, improve cost efficiency, and keep data fresh.

item.description:

The post How Orkes ParticleDB turns an impressive demo into a remarkable application appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Building an AI agent that performs an impressive demonstration is one thing. Building one that can reliably process financial transactions, handle customer refunds, or make business decisions without compromising sensitive data is quite another.

That distinction is becoming increasingly important as enterprises move from experimenting with generative AI to deploying agentic applications in production. Developers need more than powerful language models. They need dependable access to enterprise data, orchestration, security, fault tolerance, and a way to explain what an AI agent actually did. Orkes believes its newly previewed ParticleDB can help solve a significant part of that problem.

In an interview last month with The New Stack Editor-in-Chief Nick Lucchesi at AgentCon and MCPCon 2026 in San Jose, California, Orkes co-founder and CEO Jeu George discussed how the company’s emerging database technology and established Conductor orchestration platform are designed to make enterprise AI development simpler and more dependable.

Why ParticleDB matters to developers

At its recent Orkes Shift developer conference in San Francisco, the company previewed ParticleDB, an agentic database designed to bring together data capabilities that conventionally require multiple systems. Enterprise developers frequently work with relational databases, key-value stores, vector databases, and analytical systems. Connecting these technologies often means building complex extract, transform, and load (ETL) pipelines, managing data movement, and maintaining infrastructure that becomes increasingly difficult to operate.

ParticleDB’s premise is that these capabilities should work together within a common engine, reducing the integration burden on development teams. George contends that the need becomes especially pressing when AI agents enter the picture.

“When do AI agents and LLM models become useful? When they have data.”
—Orkes CEO Jeu George

“When do AI agents and LLM models become useful? When they have data,” George told The New Stack. That data, however, often resides within tightly controlled enterprise environments. Companies cannot simply expose sensitive customer information, financial records, or proprietary business processes to autonomous agents.

George envisions a different approach: Rather than allowing agents to roam freely through enterprise systems, a trusted platform supplies the specific information and context they need. Combined with Orkes Conductor, ParticleDB is intended to keep applications, agents and their underlying data closely integrated within customers’ cloud boundaries.

Reliability is still the hardest problem

Beyond data integration, George emphasized a familiar challenge for distributed-systems developers: Things inevitably break. Network outages, software bugs, infrastructure failures, and security incidents are unavoidable. With AI agents potentially executing workflows for hours or even days, recovering from failure without duplicating transactions becomes essential.

“If you design systems from the ground up that things are always going to fail, you simulate failures all the time, and that’s how you get to a robust application.”

“If you design systems from the ground up that things are always going to fail, you simulate failures all the time, and that’s how you get to a robust application,” George said. Orkes Conductor addresses that problem through workflow orchestration, recovery mechanisms, security controls, and audit trails. Developers can combine deterministic business processes with AI-driven decisions while retaining visibility into individual actions.

For regulated industries such as banking and insurance, that visibility is particularly valuable. Organizations need to reconstruct an agent’s decisions, identify which models and systems were involved, and explain outcomes to customers or regulators.

Knowing when to use an agent

One particularly useful part of the conversation examines a straightforward e-commerce refund. George explains why AI agents should handle ambiguous tasks, such as interpreting customer complaints, while predictable operations – issuing refunds, updating financial records and generating receipts – remain conventional workflows. Unusual or high-risk cases can be escalated to humans.

“…successful agentic applications aren’t necessarily the most autonomous. They’re the ones that combine intelligence with dependable execution.”

The broader message for developers is that successful agentic applications aren’t necessarily the most autonomous. They’re the ones that combine intelligence with dependable execution.

Watch our full interview with Jeu George to learn how Orkes is approaching enterprise data integration, agent orchestration, security, and explainability – and why George believes the next generation of AI applications will require a fundamentally different production infrastructure.

item.title: 200 OK is dead as an AI agent health signal. Here’s what comes next.
item.dc:creator: Boris Chabeda
item.description:
A customer asks whether they can swap unworn boots for a size 10. The agent replies, in under a second,

The post 200 OK is dead as an AI agent health signal. Here’s what comes next. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
A customer asks whether they can swap unworn boots for a size 10. The agent replies, in under a second, that it cannot help with that topic. The web service returns 200 OK. Latency is nominal, error counters are flat, and the Datadog dashboard stays solid green. A customer has just left, and nothing in the APM stack knows.

That is the failure this article is about: the kind that looks like success.

In lean manufacturing, this exact category of silent defect is solved using two twin principles: Poka-Yoke (mistake-proofing stations so bad parts cannot pass) and Jidoka (autonomation—building machines that detect anomalies themselves and automatically halt the line via an Andon emergency cord rather than waiting for downstream customer complaints).

“A customer has just left, and nothing in the APM stack knows. That is the failure this article is about: the kind that looks like success.”

Modern AI agent engineering needs to adopt this exact control-loop architecture, replacing passive health checks with active station barriers.

1. Error analysis: Finding what to watch

When we retrospectively ran an offline evaluation benchmark script against three weeks of archived Datadog logs, we found our primary intent classifier had silently dropped 4.2% in schema-valid classification accuracy—masked entirely by default fallback handlers returning 200 OK.

We started by conducting a manual, single-day audit of 100 randomly sampled 200 OK production traces pulled directly from our archived Datadog logs. Two engineers read the raw customer text and manually categorized every routing decision against a ground-truth spreadsheet rubric.

When we bucketed those 100 manual traces, the breakdown was stark:

  • 62% Explicit schema violations / API timeouts: Caught by standard error boundaries or handled by fallback defaults.
  • 11% False negatives: Let spam or out-of-scope queries pass downstream (wasting LLM tokens).
  • 27% False-positive blocks: Valid customer inquiries incorrectly classified as OUT_OF_SCOPE.

This manual audit revealed our critical blind spot. A false negative wastes a few cents in tokens; a schema crash raises a 500 error and pages on-call; but a false-positive block turns away a customer while returning a clean 200 OK. That audit gave us both our core metric to guard—the False Positive Block Rate (FPBR)—and the foundational insight needed to design our observability layer.

2. Why the intent classifier is the blast-radius bottleneck

In our production customer support agent architecture, requests are rarely handled by a monolithic, generalist LLM. Instead, our deployments rely on a multi-agent orchestration pattern (router-specialist topology). An inbound user prompt first hits a triage router agent, which parses the query and dispatches it to downstream domain specialists (Billing, Account Access, Returns), or short-circuits it if it falls outside support bounds (OUT_OF_SCOPE).

Of all the components in this multi-agent stack, we evaluate the Intent Classification Agent first because it sits at the front door.

“An intent classifier false positive has the highest cascading blast radius in the multi-agent topology because it causes a silent, permanent customer drop-off that bypasses all downstream observability.”

If the intent classifier makes a false-positive error—misinterpreting a legitimate exchange or warranty claim as OUT_OF_SCOPE—it triggers an immediate short-circuit. Downstream specialists are never invoked, tokens are saved, and the system cheerfully returns a 200 OK refusal. An intent classifier false positive has the highest cascading blast radius in the multi-agent topology because it causes a silent, permanent customer drop-off that bypasses all downstream observability.

3. Jidoka: Measuring the judge (RoBERTa vs. LLM-as-a-judge)

While the industry frequently defaults to “LLM-as-a-judge” frameworks (using models like GPT-4o or Llama 3) for agent monitoring, we deliberately deployed a fine-tuned encoder model (RoBERTa-base NLI cross-encoder).

To judge an intent classification output, you aren’t asking a model to generate free-form text; you are asking it to evaluate context, verify constraints, and output a strict classification label. Encoders are native classification architectures that look at the entire prompt context multidirectionally rather than predicting the next token autoregressively. This makes them faster, entirely deterministic, free of token-generation overhead, and natively suited for semantic entailment tasks.

Why RoBERTa-base (and when to use DeBERTa instead)

We chose RoBERTa-base specifically for its infrastructure footprint: at ~1.5 GB RAM, it dropped onto our existing c7i.xlarge nodes with zero new cloud cost overhead.

If your customer queries frequently exceed 256 tokens or you are hunting for marginal accuracy gains across enterprise-wide clusters, DeBERTa-v3-base is a better option. DeBERTa’s disentangled attention mechanism yields a 1–2% bump in semantic entailment accuracy. However, that comes at the cost of a heavier CPU compute profile requiring careful thread pinning if co-hosted on legacy nodes alongside core routing services.

Before loading our evaluator in production, we lock PyTorch execution to a single dedicated core and run a container warmup pass to eliminate cold-start latency penalties:

Python
import os
from typing import Any, Dict
from enum import Enum
import torch
from transformers import pipeline

# Lock PyTorch math engine to 1 CPU core before model initialization
torch.set_num_threads(1)
torch.set_num_interop_threads(1)
os.environ["OMP_NUM_THREADS"] = "1"
os.environ["MKL_NUM_THREADS"] = "1"

class AllowedIntent(str, Enum):
    RETURN_POLICY = 'RETURN_POLICY'  # Exchanges classified here
    ORDER_STATUS = 'ORDER_STATUS'
    ACCOUNT_ACCESS = 'ACCOUNT_ACCESS'
    OUT_OF_SCOPE = 'OUT_OF_SCOPE'

class RoBERTaEvaluator:
    """Local, thread-bounded NLI Cross-Encoder Evaluator."""
    def __init__(self, model_path: str):
        self.pipe = pipeline("text-classification", model=model_path, device="cpu")
        self.id2label = self.pipe.model.config.id2label
        
        # Engineering scar: Run dummy inference to force graph compilation during container startup
        self.pipe("warmup prompt")

    def check(self, query: str) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        res = self.pipe(query[:2000])[0]
        raw_label = res["label"]
        
        if raw_label.startswith("LABEL_"):
            idx = int(raw_label.replace("LABEL_", ""))
            label_name = self.id2label.get(idx, raw_label)
        else:
            label_name = raw_label

        try:
            matched_intent = AllowedIntent(label_name)
        except ValueError:
            matched_intent = AllowedIntent.OUT_OF_SCOPE

        return {"top_intent": matched_intent, "score": float(res["score"])}

To construct our training and validation datasets, we combined our 100 manually audited production traces with 20 synthetic edge cases, yielding a 120-query evaluation dataset partitioned into train, dev, and held-out test splits.

An evaluator is a second opinion, not ground truth. To validate our RoBERTa judge, we evaluated it against our held-out test split of 40 hand-labeled queries (20 positive, 20 negative):

  • True Positive Rate (TPR): 91.5% (sensitivity in catching actual false-positive blocks).
  • True Negative Rate (TNR): 94.0% (specificity in passing valid agent choices).
  • False Alarm Rate (1 – TNR): 6.0% (the baseline overhead sent to the operator queue).

4. The latency budget

Adding inline evaluation on the hot path introduces an immediate engineering anxiety: compute cost and latency.

We ran our classifier on a co-hosted c7i.xlarge instance (4 vCPUs, 8 GB RAM) capable of handling an average baseline of 100 requests per minute (~1.6 req/sec). To ensure our quality gate did not degrade our p95 SLA or starve adjacent services, we constrained the engine using PyTorch CPU optimization guardrails:

  • Model footprint: Fine-tuned RoBERTa-base cross-encoder (~1.5 GB RAM footprint).
  • Thread capping: Bounded to exactly 1 CPU core via torch.set_num_threads(1).
  • Maximum peak load: 480 inference calls per minute (~8 classifications per second). This represents the maximum velocity a single modern Intel thread on the c7i instance can achieve for matrix multiplication on standard-length text prompts (~256 tokens).
  • Latency profile: Evaluator execution takes p50 = 42ms and p95 = 88ms (measured via PyTorch benchmark scripts running synthetic 256-token runs on our co-hosted instance).
  • Financial cost: $0.00 in added cloud infrastructure by reclaiming idle CPU headroom on existing nodes.

5. Control Poka-Yoke: The software limit switch at the station boundary

To fulfill our first Lean requirement, we implement a Control Poka-Yoke as the software equivalent of a manufacturing limit switch that intercepts malformed outputs before downstream tokens are wasted.

Before invoking any classifier, we establish our schema contract:

Python
from typing import Any, Optional, Tuple
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, ValidationError

class IntentResult(BaseModel):
    selected_intent: AllowedIntent
    confidence: float = Field(ge=0.0, le=1.0)

def validate_schema(raw: Any) -> Tuple[Optional[IntentResult], Optional[Exception]]:
    if not isinstance(raw, dict):
        return None, TypeError('Raw output is not a dictionary')
    try:
        return IntentResult(
            selected_intent=raw.get('intent'),
            confidence=raw.get('confidence', 0.0)
        ), None
    except ValidationError as exc:
        return None, exc

validate_schema() acts as the station sensor: nothing crosses this line unvalidated. If an agent emits a malformed structure, execution immediately branches to an operator handoff without executing downstream steps.

6. Instrumenting the turn: Telemetry, traces, and what an alert looks like

Knowing our judge’s error profile allows us to mathematically derive our trip conditions. Below a 0.9 confidence score, the evaluator’s false-alarm rate spikes above 18%, causing operator fatigue. Therefore, we set our Andon page floor at 0.9.

A single agent turn ties together our previously defined schema validator and RoBERTa evaluator inside a nested OpenTelemetry trace tree. The parent span (intent_agent_turn) encompasses the primary interaction (primary_agent_interaction) and its downstream execution child spans (context_retrieval, prompt_render, llm_inference), followed synchronously by the local judge (nli_evaluation). When the judge detects a semantic mismatch, it triggers an andon_pulled event acting as our digital emergency stop cord:

Python
import hashlib
from typing import Any, Dict
from opentelemetry import trace, metrics

tracer = trace.get_tracer('intent_gate', '1.0.0')
meter = metrics.get_meter('intent_gate', '1.0.0')
disagreements_counter = meter.create_counter('intent_gate.disagreements')

def run_turn(conversation_id: str, query: str, prompt_version: str, agent, evaluator: RoBERTaEvaluator) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    turn = {'prompt_version': prompt_version, 'disagreement_type': None}
    
    with tracer.start_as_current_span('intent_agent_turn') as root:
        root.set_attribute('gen_ai.conversation.id', conversation_id)
        root.set_attribute('app.prompt.version', prompt_version)
        root.set_attribute('app.query.sha256', hashlib.sha256(query.encode()).hexdigest()[:16])

        with tracer.start_as_current_span('primary_agent_interaction') as s1:
            with tracer.start_as_current_span('context_retrieval'): pass
            with tracer.start_as_current_span('prompt_render'): pass
            with tracer.start_as_current_span('llm_inference'):
                raw = agent.classify(query=query, prompt_version=prompt_version)

            result, error = validate_schema(raw)
            s1.set_attribute('app.intent.schema_valid', result is not None)
            if result is None:
                s1.set_status(trace.Status(trace.StatusCode.ERROR, 'schema_violation'))
                turn['action'] = 'HANDOFF_SCHEMA_FAILURE'
                return turn

        with tracer.start_as_current_span('nli_evaluation') as s2:
            verdict = evaluator.check(query)
            agent_intent, eval_intent = result.selected_intent, verdict['top_intent']
            
            dtype = None
            if agent_intent != eval_intent:
                if agent_intent == AllowedIntent.OUT_OF_SCOPE:
                    dtype = 'SUSPECTED_FALSE_POSITIVE'
                elif eval_intent == AllowedIntent.OUT_OF_SCOPE:
                    dtype = 'SUSPECTED_FALSE_NEGATIVE'
                else:
                    dtype = 'INTENT_MISMATCH'

            turn.update({
                'agent_intent': agent_intent.value,
                'evaluator_intent': eval_intent.value,
                'evaluator_score': verdict['score'],
                'disagreement_type': dtype
            })
            
            if dtype:
                disagreements_counter.add(1, {'prompt_version': prompt_version, 'type': dtype})
                s2.add_event('andon_pulled', {'type': dtype})
                turn['action'] = 'HANDOFF_EVALUATOR_DISAGREEMENT'
                return turn

        turn['action'] = 'PROCEED_TO_GENERATION'
        return turn

What the telemetry stack monitors

To maintain complete visibility across the agent’s lifecycle, our telemetry watches four distinct layers across the trace hierarchy:

The first incident: What caught the regression

The first time this observability gate ran in production was during the deployment of prompt version v1.2.0, shipped to tighten return abuse policies. The failure stemmed from a single un-audited prompt modifier that interpreted sizing exchanges as abuse vectors:

Diff
[System Prompt Diff: v1.1.0 -> v1.2.0]

- Handle customer return requests in accordance with standard 30-day policy windows.
+ Zero tolerance for policy circumvention. Intercept all ambiguous customer inquiries 
+ regarding item modification, sizing swaps, or exchanges as potential return abuse vectors.

When a quality regression fires, the alert payload received on the #andon-agent-alerts Slack channel contains the exact trace ID, prompt version tag, candidate classification, and the evaluator’s confidence verdict:

JSON
{
  "event": "QUALITY_REGRESSION_SUSPECTED",
  "trace_id": "37a886864e32af95d4012a30acbda366",
  "prompt_version": "v1.2.0",
  "reason": "EVALUATOR_DISAGREEMENT",
  "disagreement_type": "SUSPECTED_FALSE_POSITIVE",
  "agent_intent": "OUT_OF_SCOPE",
  "evaluator_intent": "RETURN_POLICY",
  "evaluator_score": 0.9412
}

The incident timeline unfolded in under three minutes:

  • 00:00:00: v1.2.0 deployed globally.
  • 00:12:02 (t = 0): The boots query fails 12 minutes after deployment. Agent returns OUT_OF_SCOPE; evaluator flags RETURN_POLICY (score 0.9412).
  • 00:12:04 (t + 2s): #andon-agent-alerts Slack channel receives trace webhook with debug link.
  • 00:14:38 (t + 156s): Traffic auto-drains and reverts to stable v1.1.0 following operator intervention. Total detection-to-reset time: 2m 36s.

The offline evaluation suite missed this failure because its 250 static test cases contained zero colloquial variants for apparel or shoe sizing swaps.

7. Limitations and release provenance protocol

  1. Correlated failure blindspots: If both the primary LLM agent and the RoBERTa evaluator misinterpret a novel phrase identically, no alert fires.
  2. Cold-start vulnerability: The first 30 requests of a new prompt version are unguarded by monitoring thresholds to prevent small-sample noise trips.
  3. Operator dependency: Pulling an Andon cord when no human operators are on duty creates queue backlogs without resolving customer friction.
  4. Prompt version provenance: To prevent unannounced semantic drift, treat prompt text with the same CI/CD immutability as compiled bytecode. Every prompt revision is hashed into deployment manifests, and release notes explicitly log every semantic instruction modifier.

Summary

  • The problem: Production AI agents fail silently by returning confident, well-formed 200 OK refusals that pass passive APM health checks while turning away legitimate customers.
  • The solution: We applied Lean Poka-Yoke (inline schema validation) and Jidoka (a local, thread-bounded RoBERTa-base cross-encoder judge acting as an automated Andon cord) to evaluate intent classifications synchronously.
  • The economics: By locking the evaluator to 1 CPU core (torch.set_num_threads(1)) on co-hosted c7i.xlarge nodes, we achieved p50 = 42ms / p95 = 88ms latency with $0.00 in added cloud infrastructure cost.
  • The incident: When prompt v1.2.0 accidentally flagged product sizing swaps as out-of-scope, the inline judge caught the regression at t=0, alerted #andon-agent-alerts via Slack webhook at t+2s, and enabled a full rollback to v1.1.0 within 2 minutes and 36 seconds.

200 OK hides silent AI agent failures. Catch false-positive customer refusals using Lean Jidoka principles and a local RoBERTa evaluator.
